passages.t: The ark comes to its place
passages.happening:
The work is finished, and Solomon brings in the gifts David had dedicated (verse 1). He gathers the elders of Israel ‘to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Zion, the City of David’ (verse 2), at the feast in the seventh month (verse 3). The Levites carry the ark and the tent and the holy things, and the king and the people offer sacrifices beyond counting (verses 4-6).

‘Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the temple, the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the cherubim’ (verse 7). Its poles stay in place (verses 8-9). ‘There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb, where the LORD had made a covenant with the Israelites after they had come out of Egypt’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This is the moment David's and Solomon's work has been aiming at. The ark had wandered: carried through the wilderness, lost to the Philistines, left for years at Kiriath-jearim, brought by David to a tent in Jerusalem. Now it enters a house that stays.

The feast of the seventh month was the Festival of Booths, a week-long autumn harvest feast when Israel lived in shelters to remember the wilderness. Kings says the temple was finished in the eighth month after seven years, so the dedication may have waited for the next feast or come just before the work was formally finished; the texts do not settle it.

Elsewhere in the ancient world, installing a god's image in a new temple was the climax of building. Israel had no image to install. The ark was a throne-footstool, and inside it were only the two tablets of the covenant given at Horeb, another name for Sinai. God was present above the ark, unseen. The poles stayed in place, as the law required, a reminder that this was the same ark that had traveled with Israel.

The phrase they are there to this day in verse 9 is copied from Kings. By the Chronicler's time the ark had long disappeared, probably lost when Babylon destroyed the temple, and the second temple's inner room stood empty. What became of it is unknown, and later legends about its hiding place are not historical evidence.
passages.later: The Letter to the Hebrews says, ‘Inside the ark were the gold jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant’ (Hebrews 9:4).
passages.hard:
Verse 10 says the ark held only the two tablets, but Hebrews 9:4 says it held the manna and Aaron's staff too. Which is right?

Exodus has a jar of manna placed before the Testimony, and Numbers has Aaron's staff placed there too, meaning near the ark. Hebrews describes the ark as containing the manna, the staff and the tablets. Verse 10, copying 1 Kings 8:9, says that by Solomon's day there was nothing in it but the tablets.

Some explain that the manna and the staff were kept inside the ark in the wilderness but were lost or removed before Solomon's time, perhaps while the ark was in Philistine hands. Others think Hebrews describes the tabernacle as Jewish tradition of its day understood it, where in could loosely include things placed with the ark. On either reading, the point of verse 10 is not an inventory. At the heart of the temple lay the covenant law, the terms of Israel's life with God.
passages.asks: At the center of the house there was no image of God, only the words of his covenant. Ask what sits at the center of your worship. And ask how much of God's word you carry with you, as the ark carried the tablets.

passages.t: One voice, and the cloud of glory
passages.happening:
The priests come out of the Holy Place, all of them consecrated whatever their divisions (verse 11). The Levite singers, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun with their sons and relatives, stand east of the altar in fine linen with cymbals, harps and lyres, with 120 priests blowing trumpets (verse 12).

‘The trumpeters and singers joined together to praise and thank the LORD with one voice’ (verse 13), singing, “For He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 13). ‘And the temple, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud’ (verse 13), ‘so that the priests could not stand there to minister because of the cloud; for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The Chronicler follows 1 Kings 8 closely but adds the singers and trumpeters. Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun headed the three guilds of musicians David had organized, and the trumpets were the priests' silver trumpets, not rams' horns.

The chapter builds to one moment. The piled-up phrases, one voice, trumpets, cymbals, instruments, lead to the song, the refrain of Psalm 136 and of David's song when the ark first came to Jerusalem. At that moment the cloud fills the house. The Chronicler has arranged it so that God's glory comes in answer to his people's united praise.

Glory, kavod, comes from a root meaning weight: honor, importance, splendor, and when used of God, his visible presence. The cloud, anan, led Israel through the wilderness, covered Sinai and filled the tabernacle. It shows that God is present and hides him at the same time. Praise, halal, is the root of hallelujah, boasting in God.
passages.later: When Moses finished the tabernacle, ‘the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle’ (Exodus 40:34). David's song had used the same words: ‘Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever’ (1 Chronicles 16:34).
passages.asks: The glory came while the singers and trumpeters praised with one voice. Ask what keeps the people you worship with from one voice. And ask whether you could stand in the presence of God's glory, or would fall back like the priests.
